Mother’s 
Musings...

Dear Terrans,
Even as the University grows endlessly in all directions, our
Terrace Club is staying rooted in what we do best.
In the kitchen and on the stage, we still crank up the volume
while staying true to our roots. We’re serving 19 meals a week,
doubling down on creative menus that they never see on Prospect.
And our social calendar remains the envy of the Street. So it’s
no wonder that Terrace continues to draw a crowd, with 133
sophomores choosing us at sign-ins this winter.
Looking ahead, the Board is focused on ensuring the club’s long-
term sustainability. We are taking care of our 1904 house, and
this winter undertook a major project to upgrade our heating
system. Making sure that "Food = Love" has a permanent home takes
work, and so we're actively seeking new volunteers among our base
of committed alumni.
There's something for everyone to do, and there are no
geographical restrictions here in 2026 (I live in California). So
if you're looking for a way to reconnect with Princeton, activate
a community of brilliant people, and secure your favorite home-
away-from-home for another generation, please drop me a note at
steve.feyer@terracefclub.org.
Food to all,
Steve Feyer '03

"Yani" was a key figure in the growth of Japanese
literature and manga in English translation. Mentzas
was born in Kobe City, Hyogo Prefecture, where his
father was Greek and his mother was Japanese. 
He served as the editorial director of Vertical, where
he was responsible for selecting, editing, and
overseeing translated works from Japanese to
English. He founded Vertical in 2001 together with
founder Hiroki Sakai, specializing in English
translations of Japanese novels and manga, before
Kodansha USA acquired the company in 2020. 
Mentzas was quoted discussing the challenges and
excitement of bringing Japanese literature to
Western readers, advocating for works that
transcend cultural boundaries and resonate with
general readers rather than only niche audiences.
He was a culturally grounded editorial director and
translator who played a key role in introducing and
shaping the presence of Japanese literary and
graphic works in the English-language publishing
world through his leadership at Vertical. 
Mentzas majored in comparative literature at
Princeton in 1994 and also earned a master's
degree in English at Columbia University.

I’m Nicole Gordon, and I’m deeply honored to step into 
the role of Club Manager for Terrace Club. It’s a significant 
moment for me, as I’m proud to be the first woman to hold 
this position in the club’s history. My background in the service 
industry has instilled a deep passion for serving and enriching 
community experiences. At Terrace, my vision is to cultivate 
an even stronger sense of belonging, transforming the club 
into a vibrant home where art, food, and music not only 
converge but truly flourish. I’m excited to work alongside our 
members and alumni to enhance this incredible legacy for 
every Terran.

Ashley Blair brings strategy, sparkle, and spreadsheets 
together in perfect harmony. With a strong foundation in 
operations, HR, accounting, fundraising, and event planning,

always with an eye for growth and meaningful impact. If you 
need someone who can wear all the hats and still throw a great 
event, she’s your person.

Mihalis Alisandratos ‘18
Mihalis is a born and raised New Yorker who spent his 
time at T informing the masses as to who would be 
regaling us with tunes that weekend (I was the sign 
guy!). After spending loving years in the warm embrace 
of our mother, he returned home to do a year of service 
teaching middle school math. After entering the fiendish 
hellscape that is corporate America, Mihalis decided 
to return to school to study ethnomusicology. Having 
played the bouzouki, or the Greek guitar, his whole life, 
Mihalis wanted to go absurdly academically deep into 
questions around the instrument, its music, and the 
people who love to play and hear it. He received his MA 
in ethnomusicology at Hunter College and is now 
beginning his PhD at the CUNY Graduate Center. 
He is also a cyclist, competing in local Central 
Park and Prospect Park races as part of 
the Foundation Cycling NY Team. He lives 
in Sunnyside, Queens with his wife Morgan 
(although not a Terran you can still find her 
in the 2018 class picture in the club!) and his 
beloved Jack Russell mix Penny.

been listening to the bands Cheekface and Parquet Courts.

often think of how when Morgan would visit me and we would

who weren’t Terrans being confused as to why this girl was 
eating a bowl of cereal while loud music was blasting and that 
always sticks out in my mind as a signifier of how much of a 
home Terrace felt like to us. OH ALSO I am one of the few 
people I know who has seen a full rendition of The Nightman

1. To prepare the salad: In a medium pan heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add 
the onion and garlic, sauteing until softened. Add the rice and stir to coat. Add 
the chicken broth, water, salt, parsley, thyme and tarragon. Bring to a boil and 
continue to boil until the level of the water just covers the rice. Cover, turn the 
heat to low and cook 20 minutes. Remove from the heat and cool slightly.
2. To prepare the dressing: In a small jar combine the olive oil, lemon juice, red-
wine vinegar, mustard, thyme, garlic, salt and pepper. Shake well until emulsified.
3. Pour the dressing over the rice. Add green onions, pickle, bell pepper, carrot, 
cucumber, romaine and pimento. Refrigerate, covered. Bring to room tempera-
ture 1 hour before serving. Adjust the seasonings if necessary.

CHEESE-TOMATO TARTE PROVENÇALE
1.  Prepare pie crust according to your favorite recipe; or use a store-bought 
pie shell – I for one will not judge you! 
2.  If you’ve made your own crust, roll it out and fit it into a 9” pie plate; trim any 
overhang and crimp the edges. 
3.  Prick your pie shell all over with a fork; line with a double layer of aluminum foil 
and fill with pie weights. Pre-bake your pie crust in a hot oven until golden (400˚  
for 12-15 minutes or according to package directions); set aside to cool and 
reduce the oven temperature to 325˚.
4.  Mix the Swiss and cheddar cheeses and spoon them into your pie crust.
5.  Slice the tomatoes in half lengthwise and then into thin wedges. Arrange 
them in a circular pattern around the edge of the tart, slightly overlapping the 
wedges. 
6. Sprinkle the salt, pepper, basil, and oregano over the tomatoes.
7 .  Melt the butter in a small saucepan; sauté the scallions for a few minutes until 
tender.
8.  Spoon the scallions into the center of the tart; top with the breadcrumbs.
9.  Bake at 325˚  for 20 minutes. Let the tart cool before slicing and serving.
Et voilà, babies – you can feel très français as you enjoy this late-summer treat. 
Bon appétit!

Dear Terrans,
As we trudge through the dog days of summer, I hope the Terrace connection 
can help you stay cool. For my part, I was never all that cool, but Terrace helped 
me pretend I was during my days on campus - with our iconoclastic culture and 
the best music around, I always held my head high knowing Terrace was there for 
weirdos like me. On the eve of my 15th Reunion, now with children of my own, I no 
longer harbor any illusions about being cool. My ongoing involvement with Terrace 
isn’t about reliving past glory days or prolonging youth - rather, I joined the Board 
because I know how important Terrace remains, empowering future generations 
of Princetonians who might feel out of place on the other side of Washington Road. 
I’m happy to play a part in keeping our little island of misfit toys above the rising 
tides of conformity - a little corner of campus where strangers and oddballs might 
creatively express themselves and challenge assumptions about what a Princeton 
education is for.
With the fall semester still a ways off, I’ve been reflecting on the past year’s 
successes for our little community and looking for ways we can improve in the year 
ahead. The current state of the club is strong - our undergraduate officers and 
staff have done a fantastic job with recruiting and supporting our membership,
From the Board

leading to a strong financial performance this past fiscal year. While many 
contributed to this success, some special credit should go to Board Treasurer 
Jasmine Jeffers ‘11 and Business Manager Ryan Krebs for their leadership. I look 
forward to working with them on improving our alumni development processes 
and establishing long term plans for our club’s fiscal stability. For our physical 
infrastructure, we’ve tackled necessary and proactive maintenance issues on the 
clubhouse and kitchen, including repairs to our historic slate roof and replacement 
of the stove, alongside the myriad minor summer projects to refresh and update 
our facilities before the students return. Our club spirit is also reinvigorated after 
welcoming back nearly 1200 alums for Reunions 2024, with several special events 
for classes on major Reunion years and a remarkable Sensemaya Afrobeat All-Stars 
jam spanning nearly twenty years of Terran musicians. After this year’s Reunions, 
I can also confidently say alumni interest in our Board of Trustees is higher than I 
can ever remember.
Looking ahead to the fall, I know we can’t just be complacent with the results from 
a single year. We must continue to sustain our community with collective effort. 
For some (hopefully more each passing year), that means a financial donation. 
Unlike other eating clubs, Terrace does not charge any alumni dues - so any 
donation at any amount can help secure our future. For others, that may mean 
volunteering their time to join our Board or a Board committee. So many folks came 
up to me at Reunions interested in getting involved, curious about what we’re 
working on but uncertain of their ability to commit to Board membership full-time. 
While we’re always on the lookout for more Board members, I know we as a Board 
can do more to engage alumni and harness their interest. I took away from those 
conversations a need to create more entryways for alumni looking to get involved, 
so I’ll be working with the Board, our undergraduate officers, and our staff to set 
goals for this upcoming academic year, and I hope to publish our first Public Board 
Roadmap this fall. My hope is that transparency about Board priorities and details 
on discrete Board projects can make it easier for alumni to get involved, and 
expand our Board’s capacity and effectiveness to drive projects to completion.
The Terrace Grad Board is an all-volunteer operation, with members that have 
real lives and obligations outside of Terrace. But it’s important to remember how 
small our community actually is and the responsibility each individual Terran has to 
keep this thing going. I hope to hear more from alumni and students about YOUR 
priorities, and always welcome your feedback and engagement. 
What projects would you like to see? What talents can you bring to our mission? 
Remember, as one of our many sayings goes, Terrace is the future - no matter how 
empty the world may seem, a new world is just as likely as the old one.
Food always,
Andrew Kinaci ‘10
Chair, Terrace Graduate Board of Trustees

Welcome to the 
Terrace Farm
 (actually it’s a Petting Zoo but knew that would get your attention)

At the end of this past spring semester, between the madness of 
finals, theses, and formals, Terrace F. Club was visited by a herd 
and flock of stress-relieving farm animals.  One by one, they stepped 
off the Backyard Buddies truck to enter the Terrace yard.  There was 
a pretty dope donkey, a couple generations of goats, a loveable lamb 
(I’ll never make lamb chops again), fluffy snuggly bunny rabbits, 
funny looking ducks (they really quacked me up), some frantic 
chickens, and of course, Ham-some, the pig.

For hours, they lingered about the Terrace grounds as slews of members 
came to mingle with our new hairy, feathery friends.  As they dined on 
the Terrace grass, I could see them gaze at each other as if to say 
“this is the best grass I’ve ever had”.   And just like that, Terrace 
had opened its magical doors to yet another worthy group of creatures.

The visit from our new friends was met with rousing approval by our 
members.  The stress, if only for a couple hours, was replaced by the 
comforting pet of a rabbit’s ears, feeding hungry chickens, hugging 
a donkey, and scratching Ham-some under his chin.  We look forward to 
making this an annual event and hope Backyard Buddies had a safe ride 
home.

Until next year, we will have to make due with our regular (not 
pettable) residents under the deck - muskrats, groundhogs, foxes, and 
our ageless feral cats.  
Ryan Krebs

It’s summertime, babies – and what makes a nicer casual warm-weather meal than 
quiche? This one is light, fluffy, and green and goes fabulously with a nice big garden 
salad :)
INGREDIENTS
1 pre-baked pie crust (see NOTES)
4 eggs
2 egg whites
3/4 cup milk
1/4 cup plain Greek yogurt
1/4 cup pesto
1/4 tsp salt
1/4 tsp black pepper
2 cups baby spinach, roughly chopped
1/2 cup grated parmesan cheese
NOTES
You can use your favorite pie crust recipe – or alternatively, you can just use a store-bought crust; I 
for one am not judging you! If you go the store-bought route, follow the package directions to pre-bake 
your crust. If you decide to use your own recipe… You all went to Princeton; I am sure you can figure 
out how to pre-bake a pie crust! Either way, you want your crust to be a lovely shade of golden-brown 
and left to cool before you proceed. Hot tip: This recipe goes especially well with a whole wheat crust.
DIRECTIONS
1. Pre-heat your oven to 375° F.
2. In a large bowl, whisk together the eggs, egg whites, milk, yogurt, pesto, salt, and 
pepper. Stir in the spinach and parmesan.
3. Place your pre-baked pie crust on a baking sheet to avoid spills. Carefully pour your 
filling into the crust. You may want to wrap the edges of your crust in tinfoil at this 
stage to prevent burning.
4. Bake until the quiche is puffed up and the center is set but still jiggly, 40-50 
minutes.
5. Remove from the oven and leave to cool fully before serving.
And there you have it, luvvies – a lean green quiche machine perfect for your next 
summer soirée!

NEW ENGLAND BERRY & CITRUS PIE 
It’s Fall, babies – and one of my favorite things about Fall is making pies. This one is deceptively simple and makes the perfect addition to any autumnal holiday meal – a nice change from the standard apple and pumpkin. And it’s pretty, too :)A real feature of this recipe is that it works with any combination of berry and citrus – as long as one is sweet and the other tart. I have successfully made cranberry-orange, blueberry-lemon, and raspberry-lime versions; and it’s come out perfectly every time – it’s an incredibly ﬂexible recipe. So choose your poison and give it a go!I recommend serving with whipped cream on the side – if you really want to get fancy, you can use your chosen citrus to ﬂavor the whipped cream… But plain works beautifully, too.
INGREDIENTSFor the crust:¼ cup butter, melted – plus a little more for the pie plate½ tsp salt1 package Biscoﬀ cookies, ﬁnely crushedFor the ﬁlling:1 packet powdered gelatin¼ cup cold water10 oz. fresh or frozen cranberries (about 2 ½ cups)*¾ cup ﬁrmly packed brown sugarJuice and zest of 1 orange*1 (13.5 oz) can evaporated milk1 tsp. grated fresh ginger2 tbsp heavy cream½ tsp almond extract (optional)¼ tsp saltWhipped cream, for serving* Feel free to substitute a diﬀerent berry and citrus combination of your choice!

DIRECTIONS1. Pre-heat oven to 350° and grease a 9” pie plate with butter.2. In a large bowl, combine your Biscoﬀ crumbs with the melted butter and salt. Press the mixture into the bottom and up the sides of the pie plate. Bake until the crust is ﬁrm, about 10 minutes. Set the crust aside to cool completely.3. Meanwhile, combine the gelatin and ¼ cup cold water in a small bowl and leave to bloom, about 10 minutes.4. In a saucepan over medium heat, combine your berries, brown sugar, juice, and zest and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring occasionally, until most of the berries have burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, about 7 minutes.5. Add your evaporated milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract (if using), and salt to the saucepan and stir to blend. Heat until steaming (but do not boil), then remove the mixture from the heat. Stir in your bloomed gelatin until it dissolves.6. Use a blender or food processor to puree the berry mixture until smooth. Strain into a bowl and discard the solids – or save them and eat them on toast like jam; it’s waste-free and delicious! – and let the mixture cool to room temperature.7 . Pour the cooled berry mixture into your prepared crust and refrigerate until completely set, at least 6 hours.Happy Harvest, luvvies!
